subject: A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints

messages.author: 0ecf805027df2ed8
messages.subject: A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I've been considering the following problem:
We observe two vectors of data (for a single period), x and y. We wish to estimate a transintion (or bridge) matrix B, such that:
 1. y=B*x
 2. each element of B is constrained to <0,1> interval
 3. the column sums of B all equal one
Typically there would be some prior knowledge of B, but as a first step I would like to start with an uninformative prior.
(This example is an abstraction of a data recovery problem).

A natural formulation of the model is in the form of the system of equations (say, for a 3x2 B matrix):
y[1] = B[1,1]*x[1] + B[1,2]*x[2]
y[2] = B[2,1]*x[1] + B[2,2]*x[2]
y[3] = B[3,1]*x[1] + B[3,2]*x[2]
(plus priors and constraints for B elements)

I am not sure how this translates to Stan notation, and whether it requires formulation of a custom likelihood function. 
I would appreciate hints regarding the coding of this model (I'm new to both Stan and Bayesian modeling - I'm actually trying to identify the possibilities of the use of Bayesian estimation in my field).

Best regards
Jakub

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
parts:
Hi Jakub,

If you declare x as:
vector[2] x;

and declare B as:
simplex[2] B[3]

then you'll have the constraints you described. See the manual for how the simplex type works.



Daniel

for (n in 1:3)
  y[n] ~ normal(dot_product(x, B[n]), sigma);

You'll need to declare a sigma.

The densities all require sigma > 0 strictly.

If you have an exact problem, you probably don't want
a statistics package. Having said that, you use the
word "observe", and if that means "measure", there's almost
always measurement error and hence noise.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
parts:
Dear Bob,
Thank you for your message.

The relationship is exact, but nevertheless B is unknown and not determined - there are more unknowns (in B) than observables (y, x) here, and hence different Bs will satisfy the relationship y=B*x.

The problem I'm trying to solve is that y and x are vectors of some economic data for industries, reported (for a single year) under two different industrial classifications. The condition sum(x)=sum(y) is guaranteed by the statistcal office that supplies the data, and in that sense I don't deal with measurement error here. The case is that the data supplier does not report the links between classifications (represented by the B matrix; the elements of this matrix actually tell what proportion of, say, output of an industry j according to one classification goes to industry i according to the other classification), which I would like to uncover and show the related uncertainty in terms of probability distribution of B (as the 1st step I assume no prior information on B, but in fact some scarce information is available - including it would be perhaps the second step).

Jakub

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
parts:
I see two possible solutions:

1. Reparametrize the problem in a subspace C such that
y=B(C)*x. Basically you will get back your transformed prior, so this is
not so useful, and may be tedious to implement too.

2. Model the correction that the data supplier performed, with latent
variables, measurement errors, and some normalization. Use examples in
the manual as a starting point. Even in this case, I am not sure what
your model strongly identifies.

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
parts:
Dear Tamas,
thank you for your suggestions. Indeed I think I will look through examples with latent variables.

As a loose comment to point 2 - I think there isn't any complex process behind the correction that the data supplier does. The issue is that they know the B, and I don't (perhaps only they operate on more disaggregated data than published).
The aim of this exercise is purely practical. Once (the joint distribution) of B is known, similar transofrmations could be simulated for different years and (under some assumptions) for different variables.


Jakub

On Thursday, January 14, 2016 at 10:24:09 AM UTC+1, Tamas Papp wrote:
I see two possible solutions:

1. Reparametrize the problem in a subspace C such that
y=B(C)*x. Basically you will get back your transformed prior, so this is
not so useful, and may be tedious to implement too.

2. Model the correction that the data supplier performed, with latent
variables, measurement errors, and some normalization. Use examples in
the manual as a starting point. Even in this case, I am not sure what
your model strongly identifies.

Best,

Tamas

On Thu, Jan 14 2016, Jakub Boratyński wrote:

> Dear Bob,
> Thank you for your message.
>
> The relationship is exact, but nevertheless B is unknown and not determined
> - there are more unknowns (in B) than observables (y, x) here, and hence
> different Bs will satisfy the relationship y=B*x.
>
> The problem I'm trying to solve is that y and x are vectors of some
> economic data for industries, reported (for a single year) under two
> different industrial classifications. The condition sum(x)=sum(y) is
> guaranteed by the statistcal office that supplies the data, and in that
> sense I don't deal with measurement error here. The case is that the data
> supplier does not report the links between classifications (represented by
> the B matrix; the elements of this matrix actually tell what proportion of,
> say, output of an industry j according to one classification goes to
> industry i according to the other classification), which I would like to
> uncover and show the related uncertainty in terms of probability
> distribution of B (as the 1st step I assume no prior information on B, but
> in fact some scarce information is available - including it would be
> perhaps the second step).
>
> Jakub
>
> On Thursday, January 14, 2016 at 9:26:19 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> The densities all require sigma > 0 strictly.
>>
>> If you have an exact problem, you probably don't want
>> a statistics package.  Having said that, you use the
>> word "observe", and if that means "measure", there's almost
>> always measurement error and hence noise.
>>
>> - Bob
>>

>> <javascript:>> wrote:
>> >
>> > The case is that y=B*x holds strictly - so that sigma would need to be
>> zero (it would seem as a workaround, but I don't know if a valid one)

>> > Jakub

>> jakub.bo...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> > thank you very much for your answer - regarding parameter constraints I
>> shall try it way you suggest.

>> > Still, I'm confused about how to represent the relationship y=B*x in the
>> Stan program (hoping to understand it from examples using the simplex
>> type).
>> >
>> > Best regards
>> > Jakub

>> > On Wednesday, January 13, 2016 at 8:00:49 PM UTC+1, Daniel Lee wrote:
>> > Hi Jakub,

>> > If you declare x as:
>> > vector[2] x;
>> >
>> > and declare B as:
>> > simplex[2] B[3]
>> >

>> > Daniel

>> > On Wed, Jan 13, 2016 at 10:55 AM, Jakub Boratyński <
>> jakub.bo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > Dear Stan users,
>> >
>> > I've been considering the following problem:
>> > We observe two vectors of data (for a single period), x and y. We wish
>> to estimate a transintion (or bridge) matrix B, such that:
>> >  1. y=B*x
>> >  2. each element of B is constrained to <0,1> interval
>> >  3. the column sums of B all equal one
>> > Typically there would be some prior knowledge of B, but as a first step
>> I would like to start with an uninformative prior.
>> > (This example is an abstraction of a data recovery problem).
>> >
>> > A natural formulation of the model is in the form of the system of
>> equations (say, for a 3x2 B matrix):
>> > y[1] = B[1,1]*x[1] + B[1,2]*x[2]
>> > y[2] = B[2,1]*x[1] + B[2,2]*x[2]
>> > y[3] = B[3,1]*x[1] + B[3,2]*x[2]
>> > (plus priors and constraints for B elements)
>> >
>> > I am not sure how this translates to Stan notation, and whether it
>> requires formulation of a custom likelihood function.
>> > I would appreciate hints regarding the coding of this model (I'm new to
>> both Stan and Bayesian modeling - I'm actually trying to identify the
>> possibilities of the use of Bayesian estimation in my field).
>> >
>> > Best regards
>> > Jakub
